Money and Banks

Oliver Snellman, August 2026

The aim of this document is to provide a gentle introduction to the modern banking system, by walking through the basic steps that gave rise to it: Collaboration, money as a distributed ledger of contributions, loans as trust in future value creation, and banks as an intermediary that transformer the properties of typical savings into typical laons. Finally, the regulator sets a reserve ratio (fraction of deposits to keep at hand) to make daily banking smooth, and a capital ratio (fraction of loans backed up with own money) to function as a risk buffer. In the end there is an interactive tool that let’s you see what happens to bank’s balance sheet when these ratios are changed. We start with fully cash system and only introduce digital money in the end.

Bilateral exchange

People work, save and spend what they individually produce. Think of self-sustaining families or hunter-gatherer groups. Trade is direct and bilateral: a barrel of ale against a sack of grain, settled on the spot. A trade requires a double coincidence of wants, both parties must want what the other has at the same time, so trading connections are few and some households stay outside trade altogether. All of this commerce could be documented in a ledger.

A trade happens only when both parties want what the other has, right now. This double coincidence is rare: few connections form and some stay outside trade.

Money: portable ledger

The ledger can be used to improve the situation, so that trade can run in cycles. The ledger documents how much value a person produced for another person in the same group with a trade. This makes it possible that A serves B, B serves C, and C serves A. Money emerges as a distributed representative of this ledger. Instead of one public ledger everyone must travel to consult prior to trade, each person carries the value of their previous entries as cash. Every bill or ounce of gold says, in effect: the holder of this bill has benefitted the group by one unit. Accepting a bill as payment is the same act as documenting the utility you provided into the ledger. Free trade lets supply and demand set the relative value of everyone’s output, reflected by the allocation of cash that results from continued trade. The coincidence of needs is no longer needed, so one-way trades appear everywhere and even those who found no barter partner can join to benefit the network.

But without borrowing, you can only spend what you have already contributed. A worker might afford a house at 70; ventures stay small because purchasing power arrives only after the work; and since it takes a generation to accumulate anything, inheritance builds dynasties.

Cash is a portable entry of the shared ledger: trade runs in cycles and everyone joins. But you can only spend what you have already contributed.

Lending: trust in future contributions

Borrowing money means spending future ledger entries you have yet to make. Savers let you use entries they have already earned, trusting that you will benefit the group later, according to your potential and promises. Now benefits can precede the work: houses are bought young, and large projects that pay off only in the future can begin.

Direct saver-to-borrower loans have a matching problem, though: sizes, time horizons and risk appetites rarely line up, so many willing savers and borrowers stay unmatched.

Lending means spending your future ledger entries, on trust, out of someone’s savings. But saver and borrower rarely match in size, timing and risk, so many stay unmatched.

Bank mediates lending

The bank steps in between: it pools money from all the savers on one side and lends to all the borrowers on the other. In doing so it performs three transformations at once, of size (many small deposits fund a few large loans), of maturity (deposits withdrawable on demand fund loans that run for decades), and of risk (a diversified loan book plus the bank’s own capital stand between defaults and depositors). Its pay for this is the interest margin.

The rest of this note looks inside that box.

The bank pools many small, short-term deposits into large, long-term loans, transforming size, maturity and risk in between, for a margin. Each loan writes two ledger entries at once, new money to spend and new debt to work off, which is how the money supply can grow.

How banks work

A bank is best understood through its balance sheet. The left side (assets) lists what the bank owns: cash reserves, loans it expects to be repaid. The right side lists claimants on the bank: customers claim their deposits and lenders claim their borrowed funds. Capital is the bank’s owners’ claim, for whatever is left of the assets after depositors and lenders are paid in full. Capital works as a risk buffer: when loans default, assets shrink, and the capital claim absorbs the loss first. The two sides of the balance sheet always match in size by construction.

The three systems below differ only in two ratios set by the regulator: how much reserves must back the deposits (reserve ratio) to make daily business smooth, and how much capital must back the loans (capital ratio) as a risk buffer.

Minimum banking

The bank only safeguards deposits and lends its own cash. Every deposit can be withdrawn at any moment and if every loan defaults, only the bank’s own money is lost. The bank does not create money. New money appears only when gold is mined or the central bank issues new notes.

Minimum banking: deposits sit safe in the vault and the bank lends only its own money. New money appears only when gold is mined or the CB prints notes.

Fractional reserve

Keeping all that cash idle in the vault is wasteful, so the 100% reserve requirement is relaxed. Now the bank lend a fraction of the depositors’ cash onwards. - Withdrawals happen all the time, so a reserve ratio (here 50%) is kept as a liquidity buffer for short-term needs. - The loan pool is now larger than capital, so the capital ratio necessarily falls below 100% (here 40%). - If loans default, capital absorbs the losses up to a point; beyond that, some deposits are lost. The mere fear of this can trigger a bank run, which is why an adequate capital ratio matters as a risk buffer. - If the lent-out cash gets redeposited at a bank, deposits multiply, up to reserves divided by the reserve ratio: the classic money multiplier. With gold-limited cash the ceiling really binds. - New cash still only comes only from gold findings or the Central Bank’s printing press.

Fractional reserve banking: the bank lends part of depositors’ cash onwards. New cash still comes only from gold or the printing press.

The modern system

Money is now mostly digital and the ratios are far more extreme. Money is fungible, so it makes no sense to ask which deposited dollar was lent forward. Instead, the sizes of deposits and capital, together with the reserve and capital requirements, dictate how many loans can be issued in the balance sheet.

  • The bank can also borrow funds to expand the loan book even further, within the upper limit set by the capital ratio.
  • A new loan is not someone’s old money handed over: it is new money, created as bits by the bank in the borrower’s account. Every loan increases the money supply, and every repayment shrinks it.
  • Money is fiat: convertibility to gold is gone. Exchange rates float on supply and demand, and the central bank can create reserves without limit, so it can always act as lender of last resort. The anchor of the system is a believable inflation target instead of a gold parity.
  • The old money multiplier narrative no longer applies, where the central bank supplies reserves on demand at its chosen interest rate. Causality reverses, loans create deposits first and the reserves follow.
  • The central bank constrains the pace of money creation through the capital requirement and the interest rate it sets on reserves.
  • Note the block proportions in the figure are kept readable; with the real ratios, reserves and capital would be smaller.

The modern system: every new loan creates an equal amount of new money and repayment destroys it. The CB constrains money creation with capital requirements and the interest rate on reserves.
